Three years later and still the cutest bread I’ve ever made.  You’re going to want to save this one! 

Here’s how to make one:
1. Prepare 2 loaves of sourdough bread dough. If you want to ensure they don’t expand as much in the oven you can replace 200 of the 1000 grams of bread flour with whole wheat flour. 
2. Split the dough and shape half into an oval and half into a circle. 
3. Finish proofing the dough ensuring it is well proved (almost pushing the edge of going over) so that the dough doesn’t burst open in spots. 
4. Preheat the oven to 420F. Line a baking sheet with parchment or a non-stick mat. Put the round loaf on top and the oval loaf directly under it. 
5. One third of the way down the oval loaf, using a bench scraper or knife, make a diagonal cut on each side of the dough in the direction of the head. Bring the arms together in a folded position. 
6. Make one vertical cut at the bottom of the oval loaf to separate the legs. 
7. Sprinkle with all purpose flour and then holding a bread lame straight up make shallow cuts all over to resemble a mummy. In the middle of the round loaf make one deeper cut across for the eyes. 
8. Place in the oven with a tray of 10-15 ice cubes on the rack underneath. Bake at 420F for 20 minutes and then 450F for an additional 15-20 minutes or until the bread sounds hollow. 
9. Add on some googly eyes or candy eyes and you’ve got yourself a mummy bread. I ran out of time last year but I was planning to hollow out his belly after baking and place my spinach artichoke dip there so if you try it send me a picture! 

Let me know in the comments if you are going to try it out! And if you’re looking for an easy same day sourdough bread comment RECIPE and I’ll send you mine!

Someone asked me how to make this loaf, so here’s the full tutorial 

Pumpkin dough:
300g flour
195g water
90g pumpkin purée
100g sourdough starter
6g salt
 

Black dough:
150g Blackery flour 
100g water
6g charcoal powder 
55g sourdough starter
3g salt

Mix both doughs, let ferment for 6 hours at 26C then roll the black dough thin, shape pumpkin dough as round, spread thin layer of water on top of black dough, put pumpkin dough inside, wrap black dough around, then place loaf into a banetton, proof overnight in the fridge.
Next day bake at 500F with steam for 15min, and 450F for 20 min without steam.

I think this might be my favorite way to eat figs. 
For the base, I used my croissant dough recipe. I gave the dough 3 single folds, rolled it to 9 mm thick, cut out 9 cm circles, proofed them, then baked with weights on top to create those perfect little wells for all the filling.

Fig Compote
• 200 g fresh figs, quartered
• 50 g sugar
• 2 tbsp water
• 1 tbsp lemon juice
• Zest of ½ lemon
• Vanilla or cinnamon, optional

Simmer everything over low heat for 10–15 minutes, until the figs are soft and jammy. Mash lightly for a more rustic texture or blend until smooth. Chill completely.

Whipped Crème Fraîche Custard
• 300 ml milk
• 3 egg yolks
• 60 g sugar
• 15 g cornstarch
• 200 g crème fraîche
• 1 tsp vanilla

Cook the milk, egg yolks, sugar, and cornstarch until you have a thick custard. Remove from the heat and whisk in the crème fraîche and vanilla. Chill completely, then lightly whip until smooth and airy.

To assemble: spoon in the fig compote → pipe the whipped crème fraîche custard → add fresh fig slices → finish with a drizzle of honey.

Everyone is judging the $60 rye bread… but have you actually tried making one?

I did.

And the entire process took me about 3 days.

Multiple stages of fermentation, carefully controlled temperatures, mixing, shaping, proofing, baking-and then you still have to wait about 24 hours before you can even slice it.

My ingredients alone were almost $9 for one loaf.

Now imagine doing this commercially in SoHo, NYC. Add labor, equipment, electricity, packaging, New York rent, and all the other costs of running a bakery. They even bring their grain from Austria.

Do I think $60 is expensive for a loaf of bread? Of course.

But after making it myself, I don’t think it’s fair to look at flour + water + salt and assume the rest is pure profit.

We’re so used to cheap industrial bread that sometimes we forget what goes into making bread slowly, traditionally, and at a very high level.

And maybe the most interesting thing about this $60 loaf isn’t whether you or I would actually pay $60 for it.

It got thousands of people talking about rye bread. About fermentation. About grain. About traditional baking. And about what handmade food is actually worth.

And I think that’s pretty amazing.

So now that you’ve seen the process… do you still think $60 for a loaf of bread is crazy?

HIGH PROTEIN and only 4 INGREDIENTS Cheesy flat bread. Ready in 30 min.
• 400 g flour
• 280–300 g kefir
• 1 tsp baking soda
• 1 tsp salt

Filling
• Grated mozzarella cheese

Instructions
Combine all ingredients to form a soft dough. Let the dough rest for 15 minutes, then divide into 6 portions. Flatten each piece, add grated cheese, seal, and gently roll out. Cook on a pan over low heat, flipping a few times, until golden and cooked through.

It’s been 10 years since I had this naan bread, and I have honestly dreamed about it ever since.

Every time I’ve gone to an Indian restaurant over the years, I’ve compared the naan and wondered if maybe I had built this one up too much in my head.

Nope. 😂

We just went back after 10 years, and I can confidently say the best naan I’ve ever eaten is at BHANCHA GHAR in Nagoya, Japan.

And I say that as a baker who makes a lot of bread and has made plenty of naan from scratch.

It’s a tiny, family-owned, hole-in-the-wall kind of place with basically no social media presence, but the naan is incredible-soft, pillowy, lightly sweet, hot from the tandoor, and stuffed with melty cheese if you want it.

One bite and I knew it wasn’t nostalgia. It really is that good.

If you’re a fellow naan lover, it is absolutely worth the stop. Take the yellow subway line from Nagoya Station to Hoshigaoka, and BHANCHA GHAR is just a couple of minutes from Exit 5. Check their hours before you go.

Comment NAAN and I’ll DM you my homemade naan recipe that’s my take on this one and if you’re in Japan, check them out on Tabelog!
